transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Li (Redwood SE), Maya Torres (BrightWave CTO), Jordan Reed (BrightWave ML Eng), Priya Singh (BrightWave SRE)

Summary:
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming responses, request params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry behaviour and idempotency, SDK examples, and next steps for a short benchmark/pilot. Customer wants cost/latency tradeoffs and security docs.

Topics:
- Hosted API overview and quick demo
- Streaming + chunking and low-latency patterns
- Parameters: temperature, max_tokens, top_p, presence/penalty
- Retries: idempotency keys, backoff, rate limits
- Integration patterns and SDK snippets
- Security/compliance questions (SOC2, data retention, KMS)

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I think we have about 40 minutes, quick intros; I'm Sofia, AE at Redwood, with Ethan our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Maya: Hi, Maya here, CTO at BrightWave, and Jordan and Priya are with me. Thanks for doing this.
[00:19] Ethan: Awesome, thanks Maya. We'll keep it practical, show the hosted API, streaming, and then dig into retries and params.
[00:28] Jordan: Great, our main goal is we want to embed chat into our analytics UI, need low latency and predictable cost.
[00:36] Priya: And from SRE we care about rate limits and graceful degradation if the API gets throttled.
[00:44] Ethan: Perfect, that maps to a few controls Redwood exposes: model selection, batching, caching and streaming. We'll demo a simple chat generation call.
[00:55] Sofia: Quick qual question, what are you running now for LLMs?
[00:59] Maya: We currently use a mix, some in-house distillations for search, and OpenAI for experiments. Latency at peak is a pain and cost is creeping up.
[01:10] Ethan: Understood — hosted API is usually fastest to get started, and you can use smaller cheaper models for most prompts, fall back to larger ones for complex queries.
[01:20] Ethan: Alright I'll share my screen, quick code snippet. (screen share noises)
[01:28] Ethan: Here's a typical chat request in our JS SDK: client.chat.create with messages array, model, and some params.
[01:36] Ethan: We'll run two modes: streaming (server-sent events) and single response. Streaming is best for perceived latency when you want tokens as they arrive.
[01:47] [01:47] Ethan: (runs example) You can see tokens streaming back, UI updates progressively. This reduces time-to-first-byte significantly.
[01:55] Jordan: Is streaming incremental tokens or partial sentences?
[01:58] Ethan: It's token-level streaming; sometimes middle of a word, depends on tokenizer. UI should handle partial tokens, then finalize when stream closes.
[02:06] Maya: Any gotchas for mobile clients?
[02:09] Ethan: For mobile we recommend a short initial response streaming to display the gist, plus later full response retrieval. Also consider connection drops - we expose chunk ids so you can resume or re-request if needed.
[02:22] Priya: You mentioned chunk ids — is that OAuth or some custom header?
[02:26] Ethan: It's a response metadata field from the streaming endpoint; your app receives event frames with seq ids. Not an auth token.
[02:33] Sofia: Let's talk params — temperature, top_p, and max_tokens.
[02:36] Ethan: Right. temperature controls randomness; set 0–1, e.g., 0.0 for deterministic, 0.7 for creative. top_p is nucleus sampling; you can combine them. max_tokens is a hard cap on generated tokens.
[02:50] Ethan: We also support presence and frequency penalties for controlling repetition.
[03:00] Jordan: For our use case we need short answers, so low max_tokens and temp about 0.2?
[03:04] Ethan: Sounds right. Also consider system messages to anchor style and role.
[03:10] Maya: How do we control cost? Any suggestions?
[03:13] Ethan: A few levers: use smaller models for high volume, enable prefix / KV caching for repeated stems, set conservative max_tokens, and batching on the server side. Redwood Optimize will give suggestions per workload.
[03:27] Maya: Nice. What's Redwood Optimize?
[03:29] Ethan: It's our recommendation engine that analyzes token breakdowns and suggests quantization, batching, cache policies, and model choices to meet cost/latency targets.
[03:38] Priya: Ok re: retries, if we see 5xxs from Redwood, what's the recommended pattern?
[03:42] Ethan: Use idempotency keys for mutation-style calls, exponential backoff with jitter for transient errors, and consider a circuit-breaker at the client. For streaming, if the connection drops we return a non-recoverable stream state so you'd re-request the message with the same idempotency key.
[03:58] Sofia: We also have built-in retry handling in our SDKs that handle 429s with backoff, but customers often implement client-side queueing for higher control.
[04:10] Jordan: Do you have recommended backoff values?
[04:13] Ethan: We suggest initial backoff 200-500ms, double each try, cap around 8-10s. For 429s respect Retry-After header if present.
[04:22] Maya: Rate limits — per-account or per-key?
[04:26] Ethan: Per-API-key with tier-based limits; for Dedicated customers we can set custom throughput. Hosted has quota and rate limits visible in the console.
[04:36] Priya: If we hit a hard limit, is there graceful fallback to a smaller model?
[04:40] Ethan: You can configure routing policies — fallback to a compatible model variant or region. That way you maintain availability at reduced quality.
[04:48] Maya: Great. Let's talk about security and data retention briefly.
[04:53] Sofia: We have SOC 2 Type II, options for data retention windows, and for private data we offer VPC/Private deployments and Enterprise keys integration with KMS/HSM.
[05:04] Jordan: For trial will hosted clear user prompts from logs?
[05:07] Ethan: We have configurable retention; by default trial logs are retained short-term, but for enterprise we can turn off logs or send to your log buckets via syslog. We'll share the security whitepaper.
[05:19] Maya: Do you support SSO and RBAC?
[05:22] Sofia: Yes, SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning, and granular RBAC in the console.
[05:28] Priya: Does the hosted flow integrate with our KMS for key rotation?
[05:32] Ethan: For hosted we integrate with cloud provider KMS for encryption at rest; for private deployments you can bring your own HSM/KMS keys.
[05:40] Jordan: Ok thanks. Back to demo — can we see a code example of retries + idempotency?
[05:45] Ethan: Sure. (types) Here's a POST with an Idempotency-Key header; the SDK will re-use that to avoid double effects, and in the body we set request_timeout and max_retries.
[05:57] Ethan: I'll run a sample that intentionally fails a couple times to show backoff, you can see attempts in the log.
[06:06] [06:06] (demo shows logs)
[06:09] Maya: Nice to see the visibility. Does console show per-route latency and token cost?
[06:14] Sofia: Yes console has per-model, per-route breakdown, token-level cost, and tracing hooks so you can correlate requests to logs.
[06:23] Jordan: Any SDKs for Java? We are mostly Node + Java microservices.
[06:28] Ethan: We have official SDKs for JS and Python; Java community SDK is in beta — you can use REST easily. We can share a Java snippet.
[06:36] Priya: For streaming are there WebSocket options?
[06:39] Ethan: Streaming via SSE (server-sent events) and websocket proxy is supported for enterprise; SSE is lightweight and works well for browsers.
[06:47] Maya: Let's talk about measured latency — do you have numbers?
[06:51] Ethan: For hosted small models token-latency can be single-digit ms per token, TTFB often under 200ms for short responses; depends on model and region. We publish latency profiles in the model catalog.
[07:05] Jordan: And price per 1k tokens roughly?
[07:09] Sofia: Pricing depends on model; we have a banded pricing page — we'll include a starter plan for you.
[07:15] Maya: For benchmarking, what inputs do you need from us?
[07:18] Ethan: Sample prompt set, expected QPS, desired latency SLO, and preferred region. We'll run a quick benchmark on hosted and share a report.
[07:27] Jordan: We'll aim to share prompts by EOD Friday.
[07:31] Priya: On error scenarios, can you mark some calls as safety filtered? We have PII concerns.
[07:36] Ethan: Yes we have content filters and you can run an offline safety pass. For PII we recommend client-side redaction plus server-side filters.
[07:45] Maya: How do webhooks for async responses work if a long job completes?
[07:49] Ethan: You can do async by polling or register a webhook; webhook retries follow typical 5xx backoff, and you get an idempotency key to ensure no duplicate processing.
[07:59] Sofia: Quick pause — any blockers to moving to a pilot?
[08:03] Maya: Need security docs and pricing. Also want to run 1-day benchmark before committing.
[08:09] Sofia: That's fine. We'll send both.
[08:12] Ethan: I'll also include a sample Node and Java curl example for streaming and retry patterns.
[08:18] Maya: One more question — do you support function or tool calling?
[08:22] Ethan: We have structured output and function-calling style patterns; that said today's demo focuses on chat/text basic. We can demo function-calling next call.
[08:33] Jordan: About regional routing — can we pin to us-west-2?
[08:36] Sofia: Yes for Hosted you can select region in the request header or set account default; for Dedicated we can pin capacity.
[08:44] Priya: For observability — can we stream logs into our Splunk?
[08:48] Ethan: Yes we support log forwarding and you can export traces. We'll include the integration guide.
[08:55] Maya: Cool. Walk me through a typical response time improvement when you turn on prefix/KV caching.
[08:59] Ethan: If you have repeated prefixes (like repeated system or user history), KV cache can reduce generation cost by reusing cached KV layers; it can drop latency for common prompts by 30-60% depending on sequence lengths.
[09:17] Jordan: Ok makes sense.
[09:19] Ethan: Another practical tip: for short UI responses use streaming with a low max_tokens and temperature 0-0.2 to keep answers concise and cheaper.
[09:29] Maya: For retries on streaming if connection drops mid-stream, do you re-request and append or dedupe?
[09:35] Ethan: You re-request the full response with same idempotency key, and client should dedupe rendered chunks using sequence ids. We give a final message checksum so you can detect duplications.
[09:48] Priya: About quota spikes, is there a way to request burst capacity?
[09:53] Sofia: For Hosted we have burst windows based on account tier; for dedicated you reserve capacity and burst policies can be configured.
[10:00] Maya: Are there sandbox limits for the trial key?
[10:03] Sofia: We'll give you a trial key with a 50k token allotment and reasonable rate limits for benchmarking.
[10:10] Jordan: Perfect.
[10:12] Ethan: Quick demo closing — here's an example curl showing SSE stream and how events look: event: token, data: {"token":"Hello"}...
[10:23] (short pause)
[10:26] Maya: That example is very helpful.
[10:29] Sofia: Alright, recap and next steps: Sofia to send pricing and plan options; Ethan to share security docs and integration guides; BrightWave to send prompt set and QPS targets; schedule benchmark next week.
[10:44] Maya: Sounds good. Any follow-up on the legal side? We have procurement that wants a draft contract.
[10:49] Sofia: We can send standard MSA and SOW templates, and our legal team can kickoff after pilot scope.
[10:57] Priya: Can we get a contact for privacy questions?
[11:00] Sofia: I'll include our security contact and CISO email in the doc bundle.
[11:06] Jordan: Great.
[11:08] Maya: Thanks team, this was useful.
[11:12] Sofia: Thanks all. We'll send the follow-ups by Thursday.
[11:16] Ethan: Thanks everyone, talk soon.

(Transcript contains occasional ASR errors and minor speaker mislabels.)
